title: When the House Falls
premise: Kestrel Pemberton, a hospice nurse who has spent twelve years in the crumbling Pemberton house pretending its noises are pipes and settling wood, notices that every mirror now lags one second behind reality—and in that lagged second, something else moves. The dying patients he tends have begun humming a counting song whose final verse, they whisper, is a door; whoever sings it aloud invites the house's original owner to wear their face. As Kestrel investigates his family's buried history, he learns he was brought to the house as a child precisely because he could hear the counting—and that his found family of fellow caretakers has been keeping him as bait. In the climax, Kestrel must learn the last verse without singing it, using it instead to unname the thing in the mirrors and free the house's trapped dead, at the cost of his own reflection and the identity he clung to.
about_author: Coral Sterling is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who writes horror drawn from the hush of hospice halls and the things houses remember. They live in a drafty Victorian with too many mirrors, all of which behave—so far.

chapters.title: The Second Behind the Glass
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. During a night shift caring for dying Mr. Aldous, Kestrel notices the hallway mirror reflecting the room a beat late—a figure standing where no one stands. He rationalizes it as exhaustion, but the emotional beat is dread cracking through twelve years of practiced denial.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Aldous dies humming a children's counting song, stopping just before the last verse. Other longtime residents admit they've heard it for decades. Kestrel realizes the dying aren't delirious—they're rehearsing. Beat: the comfort of routine curdles into complicity.

chapters.title: House Rules
chapters.summary: POV: Marisol, the housekeeper who raised Kestrel after his parents vanished. She quietly enforces odd rules—cover mirrors at dusk, never answer knocking after three. Her chapter reveals she loves Kestrel but is hiding something about why he was brought here. Beat: loyalty shown through concealment.

chapters.title: What the Lag Shows
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Experimenting with a hand mirror, Kestrel sees the lagged room: furniture arranged as it was fifty years ago, and a tall figure in an old-fashioned coat turning toward him. The lag widens to two seconds. Beat: curiosity overriding fear, the first active step toward truth.

chapters.title: The Found Family
chapters.summary: POV: Dev, the young live-in aide Kestrel considers a brother. Dev's warmth is genuine, but he reports Kestrel's mirror experiments to someone via notes left in the dumbwaiter. Beat: tenderness braided with betrayal the reader sees before Kestrel does.

chapters.title: Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In the attic, Kestrel finds a caretaker's ledger listing every resident since 1911—including 'K. Pemberton, age 6, delivered per agreement.' His childhood arrival was contractual. Beat: identity shaken; the house chose him before he chose it.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A new dying patient, Mrs. Okonkwo, teaches him the song's verses: each one counts down a year of the house's history. She refuses to teach the last, warning that singing it is an invitation. Beat: knowledge as both gift and trap.

chapters.title: Marisol's Confession
chapters.summary: POV: Marisol. She remembers the previous 'hearer,' a boy named Tomas who sang the last verse in 1979 and was replaced within a month—his face worn by something else until it frayed. She has kept Kestrel ignorant to keep him safe. Beat: love that lies.

chapters.title: Two Seconds Gone
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The lag stretches; now Kestrel glimpses himself in the delayed reflections doing things he hasn't done yet—singing. The lagged self knows the last verse. Beat: horror of recognizing your own face as a stranger's mask.

chapters.title: The Dumbwaiter Answers
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel finds Dev's notes and follows the dumbwaiter shaft to a sealed parlor where offerings—hair, photographs, names—are left for 'the Resident.' He understands he is livestock. Beat: betrayal detonating; found family revealed as feeding arrangement.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Parlor
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel confronts Dev and Marisol together. Dev confesses the household has fed the Resident a 'hearer' every generation to spare everyone else; Marisol admits she was meant to prepare Kestrel, not protect him. Beat: rage, then the harder question—if not this, what?

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Last Night
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Sitting vigil, Kestrel hears the Resident use Okonkwo's failing voice to sing four verses perfectly. She dies smiling, freed. Kestrel realizes the song isn't a summoning—it's a leash, and the last verse might cut either way. Beat: grief sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Tomas in the Walls
chapters.summary: POV: interlaced voices—the house's trapped dead, including Tomas, speaking through cold spots and tapping. They reveal the Resident was the first Pemberton, who bound his family into the walls to avoid death and needs a living singer to renew the binding. Beat: the monsters have victims' faces.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel begins memorizing the last verse from Okonkwo's notes—reading only, never voicing it. Each silent rehearsal leaves frost on his lips and erases a memory: his mother's face, his own birthday. Beat: the price of the weapon is the self.

chapters.title: Dev's Choice
chapters.summary: POV: Dev. Torn between the household's covenant and his love for Kestrel, Dev burns his notes and offers to take Kestrel's place if it comes to singing. Kestrel refuses to let anyone be bait again. Beat: found family redefined—not blood or duty, but chosen sacrifice refused.

chapters.title: The House Closes
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Doors vanish, windows show 1954, and the lag swallows whole rooms. The Resident, wearing Kestrel's lagged reflection, walks the halls in his body's shape, practicing the last verse in his voice. Beat: claustrophobic escalation; nowhere left to hide or deny.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV: Marisol. She offers herself to the Resident as a hearer in Kestrel's stead, using her fifty years of service as claim. The Resident accepts—but a bargain with it is never simple, and her name begins fading from every photograph. Beat: loyalty pushed to its terrible limit.

chapters.title: The Mirror Room
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel enters the mirrored ballroom where the Resident waits, wearing Marisol's fading face and offering a trade: sing the verse, keep your memories, save Marisol. Every mirror shows versions of Kestrel who said yes. Beat: temptation staged as compassion.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Unspoken
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Climax. Kestrel mouths the verse silently while the Resident sings it aloud, completing the binding onto itself. The trapped dead rise through the mirrors and speak their names, unraveling the Resident's borrowed faces. Kestrel's reflection shatters rather than submit. Beat: victory through refusal, paid in glass and selfhood.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Glass
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Dawn. The house is ordinary—pipes, dust, honest silence. Marisol survives but doesn't remember Kestrel's name; the memories he spent don't return. Mirrors show rooms on time, and no one in them. Beat: hollow relief, mourning what was traded.

chapters.title: What Remains of Kestrel
chapters.summary: POV: Dev. Dev cares for the diminished Marisol and a quieter Kestrel, who no longer hears the counting—or much else of his past. But when a dying patient hums the song's first verse, Kestrel still turns toward the sound. Beat: identity rebuilt from choice, not memory.

chapters.title: One Second Early
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Final image: packing to leave, Kestrel passes the hall mirror and catches his reflection moving a second before he does—then settling, waiting, watching kindly. He smiles, says 'not today,' and walks out into the light. Beat: ambiguous peace; the house falls, but something patient remains.
